column1: Children in developing countries are healthier and more likely to survive past the age of five when their mothers can read and write.
column2: 在发展中国家，母亲会读写的孩子更健康，也更有可能活过五岁。

column1: Experts in public health accepted this idea decades ago, but until now no one has been able to show that a woman’s ability to read in itself improves her children’s chances of survival.
column2: 公共卫生专家几十年前就接受了这个观点。不过，直到这项研究之前，还没人能证明母亲识字本身能提高子女的存活机会。

column10: chances of survival|n. 存活的机会

column1: Most literate women learnt to read in primary school, and the fact that a woman has had an education may simply indicate her family’s wealth or that it values its children more highly.
column2: 多数识字女性是在小学学会阅读的。女性受过教育这一事实，可能仅仅说明她家境较好，或是她的家人更看重孩子。
column6: may simply indicate|可能只是表明

column1: Now a long-term study carried out in Nicaragua has eliminated these factors by showing that teaching reading to poor adult women, who would otherwise have remained illiterate, has a direct effect on their children’s health and survival.
column2: 尼加拉瓜的一项长期研究排除了这些因素的影响。研究表明，教那些原本会一直不识字的贫困成年女性阅读，会直接影响她们孩子的健康和生存。
column7: poor adult women|n. 贫困成年女性

column1: In 1979, the government of Nicaragua established a number of social programmes, including a National Literacy Crusade.

column8: National Literacy Crusade|n. 全国扫盲运动

column1: By 1985, about 300,000 illiterate adults from all over the country, many of whom had never attended primary school, had learnt how to read, write and use numbers.
column2: 到1985年，全国各地已有约30万名不识字的成年人学会了读写和算数，他们中许多人从未上过小学。
column6: from all over the country|来自全国各地

column1: During this period, researchers from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, the Central American Institute of Health in Nicaragua, the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua and the Costa Rican Institute of Health interviewed nearly 3,000 women: some of whom had learnt to read as children, some during the literacy crusade and some who had never learnt at all.
column2: 在这一时期，来自利物浦热带医学院、尼加拉瓜的中美洲卫生研究所、尼加拉瓜国立自治大学和哥斯达黎加卫生研究所的研究者，访谈了近3000名女性。有的儿童时期就学会了阅读，有的是在扫盲运动中学会的，还有的从未学会阅读。

column1: The investigators’ findings were striking.

column1: In the late 1970s, the infant mortality rate for the children of illiterate mothers was around 110 deaths per thousand live births.

column1: For those women who learnt to read through the campaign, the infant mortality rate was 84 per thousand, an impressive 21 points lower than for those women who were still illiterate.

column1: The children of the newly-literate mothers were also better nourished than those of women who could not read.

column1: Why are the children of literate mothers better off?

column1: According to Peter Sandiford of the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, no one knows for certain.

column1: They are working with the same group of 3,000 women, to try to find out whether reading mothers make better use of hospitals and clinics, opt for smaller families, exert more control at home, learn modern childcare techniques more quickly, or whether they merely have more respect for themselves and their children.

column1: The Nicaraguan study may have important implications for governments and aid agencies that need to know where to direct their resources.

column1: Sandiford says that there is increasing evidence that female education, at any age, is ‘an important health intervention in its own right’.

column1: The results of the study lend support to the World Bank’s recommendation that education budgets in developing countries should be increased, not just to help their economies, but also to improve child health.

column1: ‘We’ve known for a long time that maternal education is important,’ says John Cleland of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.
